segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Isha in the original: kurvann eveha, doing, just here, and work that doesn't stick. The very next verse drops into the dark.

Scroll long enough and something is always for sale: more followers, a bigger room, a better face. The Isha has just finished a verse about a long, working life, and now it turns, hard, toward what all that grabbing can cost. Asurya nama te loka andhena tamasavritah. Worlds known as sunless, covered in blind darkness. The verse is short and stark, and it has one word that needs reading slowly: the word for who goes there.
screen: `ALWAYS SOMETHING FOR SALE.` → `WORLDS COVERED IN BLIND DARKNESS.` → `WHO GOES THERE?`

segments.voice: The question: what does it cost to forget your own self? The Isha's answer comes in one word: atmahano. Atman, self, and han, to strike. Self-slayers. Shankara, the old commentator, reads it as people who live as if the deep self weren't there, who bury it under grabbing and forgetting. That fits the verses around it: let go, don't grasp, work that doesn't stick. And the verse's last word is janah, people. Not monsters. People who forgot. A neighbor tradition asks almost the same question. In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus says: For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Here's what the two share: a warning that you can win everything on offer and lose the one who was doing the winning. Here's an honest difference. In Mark, the soul is a person's own life, given by God and answerable to God. In Shankara's reading of the Isha, the atman is the deep self, which his school holds is one with Brahman, the ground of everything. The two neighbors pose the same question. They don't mean the same thing by the self, and neither needs to borrow the other's answer. If the word self-slayers lands heavier than that today, 988 in the US, or local emergency help elsewhere, is there to call or text.
screen: `ATMAHANO: ATMAN + HAN.` · `PEOPLE WHO FORGOT.` · `MARK: GAIN THE WORLD, LOSE THE SOUL.` · `ONE QUESTION, TWO SELVES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the dark behind the lids be only dark, nothing to fear. With each breath, notice the one who is noticing: still here, unhurt, not for sale. When a thought tries to sell you something, let it pass, and come back to the one who noticed it.
Reading the Isha in the original, verse three: worlds known as asurya, sunless, and atmahano, those who forget the self, read the way Shankara reads it.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers who follow Shankara read this verse as a warning against ignoring the self, not as a curse; it is read alongside the verses on letting go before it.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Mark 8:36 (KJV, quoted) as the neighbor. Shared: winning everything and losing the self. Honest difference: in Christian teaching the soul is the person's own life before God; in Shankara's Advaita the atman is one with Brahman. A Christian reader and a Hindu Keeper should both confirm the difference is fairly put and ranks neither. 'His school holds' attributes the identity claim to Advaita only, not to all Hindus.
